help.body:
Description
Machine MSA Analysis

Purpose
Machine MSA (Measurement System Analysis) evaluates whether an automated measurement system — such as a CMM, laser scanner, or in-line gauge — is capable of producing measurements that are accurate and consistent enough for production control and quality decisions. Following the AIAG MSA 4th Edition standard, it quantifies how much of the observed variation in measurements comes from the measurement system itself (bias and repeatability) versus real part-to-part differences, and tests whether any systematic offset exists between the machine's readings and a traceable reference standard.

Inputs
Reference/standard value (required) — the certified reference measurement for each part, typically from a calibrated master gauge or CMM traceable to a national standard

Measurement/response or Bias (at least one required) — either the raw machine measurements, or the pre-computed bias (machine minus reference); if raw measurements are supplied the bias is computed automatically

Appraiser/Operator (optional) — if multiple operators run the machine, this column identifies who took each measurement; when supplied the analysis partitions variation into repeatability (within-operator) and reproducibility (between-operator) components

Tolerance Range (USL − LSL) (required) — the full engineering tolerance for the characteristic being measured; used to express measurement system error as a percentage of the allowable part variation

Target (optional) — the nominal design value; when provided, the Probability of Misclassification plot displays actual part dimension coordinates (e.g. LSL = 5.00 mm, USL = 7.00 mm) rather than centred coordinates

Historical process standard deviation (optional, strongly recommended) — a known long-run process SD from a stable production baseline; when supplied the Variation Ratio is expressed as a percentage of true process capability (%Process); when omitted the study parts' own variation is used instead and a warning is displayed (%Study)

Gage Name, Date of Study, Study performed by (optional) — metadata displayed in the report header

Output Interpretation
The analysis produces a summary stats, a few plots and a correlation scatter plot

Summary stats shows the key acceptance metrics. MS Standard Deviation (GRR SD) is the combined measurement system spread including both repeatability and reproducibility.

95% Uncertainty is the half-width of the measurement uncertainty band on a single reading.

The GRR %Tolerance acceptance meter is the primary AIAG acceptance criterion: below 10% is acceptable, 10–30% is marginal and requires engineering judgement, above 30% is unacceptable and the gauge must be improved before use in production.

The GRR %Process (or %Study) meter expresses the same measurement error relative to process capability.

The Probability of Misclassification plot shows the risk of making wrong accept/reject decisions near the spec limits — the Alpha Risk curve (blue) shows the probability of rejecting a good part, and the Beta Risk curve (orange) shows the probability of accepting a bad part; both should be as close to zero as possible in the middle of the spec range and rise sharply only at the boundaries.

The Percent Contribution pie chart shows what fraction of total variation comes from the measurement system versus real part differences; a well-capable gauge should contribute less than 1–2% of process variance.

Additional Bias plot options, if clicked, shows the IM-R (Individuals and Moving Range) chart of the bias values — points outside the control limits indicate unstable measurement performance that should be investigated before the study results are used.

The Difference by Reference scatter checks whether bias changes systematically across the measurement range, which would indicate a linearity problem.

The Difference by Operator interval plot compares bias distributions across operators — overlapping intervals with means near zero indicate no significant operator effect.

The t-test for bias, if additional bias stats option is clicked, in the output tests whether the average difference between machine and reference is statistically distinguishable from zero; a significant result (p < 0.05) means the machine has a systematic offset and should be recalibrated.
The ANOVA table (shown when operators are present) tests whether different operators produce meaningfully different bias levels; a non-significant result (p > 0.05) confirms the measurement process is robust to operator identity.
